tasks.title: THE BEST LONDON MARKETS
body: Whatever you're looking for, you'll find it at the best markets in London.

Come with an empty stomach and discover a gourmet's paradise at Borough Market near London Bridge. Find stacks of fresh and organic produce, as well as condiments, baked treats and delicious street food. Regular three-hour Borough Market Food Tours led by knowledgeable experts explain the history of the area, while you tuck into delicious food and drink fresh from the market.

Located around the historic Market Building, Covent Garden Market features a range of stalls and specialty shops, as well as entertainment outside the market from opera singers to magicians. This central London shopping market is an architectural masterpiece including toy shops, perfume boutiques, restaurants and cafés.

Feeling peckish? Then take a stairway straight to foodie heaven at Market Hall Oxford Street, the UK's largest food hall filled with everything from sweets to savouries. Three floors of eager traders are ready to serve delicious bites seven days a week in the West End.

One person’s junk is another’s gem – and you will find plenty of both at this east London market spread across several streets. At Brick Lane Market, you can pore over second-hand furniture, vintage clothes, shoes and lots more. Sunday is the best day to visit, with Upmarket featuring more than 200 stalls.

Soak up the atmosphere at one of the oldest markets in London on Portobello Road. There has been a market here since the 1800s, offering a great variety of products. Although open every day except Sunday, the market is in full swing on Saturdays when there can be more than 1,500 stalls to browse.

Go bananas for Seven Dials Market, an ex-banana warehouse turned glass-roofed chillout spot full of delicious food on every corner. Head downstairs if you're in need of a bite of street food, or upstairs for elegant terrazzo countertop cafes.

Located beneath the vaulted arches of London Bridge, the foodie paradise of Maltby Street Market comes to life every weekend. There's a fantastic range of street food, from delicious Chinese dumplings at Gyoza Guys, to Amen Ethiopian Cuisine and La Pepia's Venezuelan street food.

tasks.title: THE UK’S NETWORK OF FREE HIKING ’HOTELS’
body: Founded in 1965, the Mountain Bothy Association is a registered charity that maintains bothies: "simple shelters in remote country for the use of all who love wild and lonely places". The organisation manages more than a hundred bothies in Scotland, Wales and Northern England. The system is simple. Bothies are free to use and open to anyone. They can't be booked in advance, and groups of six or more and commercial groups are asked not to use them. As long as you respect other users, the bothy and its surroundings, you're welcome.

Every bothy is an adapted building with a previous life. Most are old shepherd's huts, sheds, farmsteads or workers' accommodation. In the early 20th century, hill farming declined and fewer and fewer people lived in remote locations, leaving many buildings behind. After World War Two, hiking and mountaineering as leisure pursuits dramatically increased in popularity and those exploring the outdoors began using these abandoned buildings as shelters.

Keeping the buildings habitable is all done by volunteers; however, bothies are by no means luxurious. You won't find electricity or running water and will be lucky to have a long-drop toilet. Most will have a stove, but there's no guarantee a supply of fuel will be there – not to mention any kitchenware. You should pack as if you're camping, including a tent in case the bothy is overcrowded or you don't fancy the company.

The company you find in bothies, and the fact that it's completely unpredictable, is one of their unique attractions, according to hikers. In a world where everything is bookable and controllable, you just have to go and turn up, and you could have it all to yourself or you could meet some incredible people and connect with them.

In 2009, the locations of the bothies were shared online by the association so that more hikers can find them, which wasn’t a unanimously popular move. Part of the hikers’ concern was that the people might begin using these spaces as places to party instead of using them for a shelter while enjoying outdoor pursuits.

tasks.title: 'MISOKINESIA’ MAY AFFECT 1 IN 3 PEOPLE, RESEARCH SHOWS
body: Misokinesia is the reduced tolerance of others’ repetitive bodily movements. Misokinesia sufferers can have an intense biological and emotional reaction to other people tapping their fingers, clicking a pen or twiddling their hair. {{0}}
The severity of people's reaction to irritating movements varies. {{23}} Others, however, may get a very strong emotional reaction – anger, panic or distress -and just can't filter them out.

One common way people try to manage the condition is by avoiding looking at fidgeting or by distracting themselves. {{24}} A lot of sufferers feel ashamed that they get such strong reactions, which can be a problem in itself, because suppressing your emotions can intensify them and make them worse.

Misokinesia sufferers often report some overlap with the sound-sensitivity of misophonia. {{25}} Dr Jane Gregory, a clinical psychologist, who has been studying both misokinesia and misophonia, told the BBC that the two go alongside each other frequently. {{26}} However, misophonia is a more recognized disorder. Obviously, people have also been experiencing misokinesia for a long time but just didn't have a name for it.

{{27}} Across a series of experiments involving over 4,100 participants, researchers concluded that one in three people might be affected by misokinesia, which causes them intense feelings of rage and disgust. {{28}} This explains a lot about why teenagers who twirl their hair or pick their nails annoy the rest of us.

The findings thus confirm that a large segment of the general population may have a visual-social sensitivity that has received little formal recognition so far. {{29}} Misokinesia could explain why open office plans often do not work out well.

tasks.title: WHY DO WE CARVE PUMPKINS AT HALLOWEEN?
body: The jack-o’-lantern has a long history with Halloween, {{0}} our favorite demonic faces haven’t always been cut out of pumpkins.

Their origin {{10}} an Irish myth about Stingy Jack, who tricked the Devil for his own monetary gain. When Jack died, God {{11}} him into heaven, and the Devil didn’t let him into hell, {{12}} Jack was sentenced to wander the earth for eternity. In Ireland, people started to carve demonic faces out of turnips to frighten away Jack’s wandering soul. {{13}} Irish immigrants moved to the U.S., they began making jack-o’-lanterns from pumpkins.

But how did jack-o’-lanterns become associated with Halloween? Halloween is based on the Celtic festival Samhain, a celebration in ancient Britain and Ireland {{14}} marked the end of summer and the beginning of the new year on November 1. It was believed that during Samhain the souls of those who had died that year traveled to the otherworld and that other souls {{15}} to visit their homes.

In the 8th century CE, the Roman Catholic Church moved All Saints’ Day, a day {{16}} the church’s saints, to November 1. This meant that All Hallows’ Eve (or Halloween) fell on October 31. Traditions from Samhain remained, such as {{17}} disguises to hide yourself from the souls wandering around your home. The folklore about Stingy Jack was quickly incorporated into Halloween, and we’ve been carving pumpkins — or turnips — ever since.
